chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 101 to 110, Ammuvanar's neythal decade told to the mother (தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து): every poem opens on the refrain அன்னை வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை and the friend lays the girl's secret love before her mother, first as cure (the chariot, its bell, the matched pair), then as symptom (gold brow, pale chest, sleepless nights), then as grievance (the shoulders he left) and a plea to fate.

101.reading: The friend tells the mother to look: the shore lord's chariot has come, tearing through the green adumbu creepers, riding up and down and trampling the neythal, the chariot that is the medicine for the sickness her daughter's flower-like kohled eyes have caught.
101.nuance: The poem names the cure before the illness is admitted: the friend does not tell the mother her daughter loves, she tells her the medicine is arriving, so the disclosure is made as a diagnosis. The chariot crushing the shore plants shows a man coming openly and in haste, not by stealth.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore creeper, the neythal and the shore lord fix the coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; நின்மகள் confirms the mother is addressed

102.reading: The friend tells the mother that in their town the bell of his chariot rings sweetly, so that the girl's suffering, unceasing as the cries of the birds of the dark-blue sea, may end.
102.nuance: Line 2 can also be read as the bell sounding without pause like the sea birds; either way the sea birds' unending noise is set against one sound that ends the noise of grief. A bell heard openly in the town is the sign of a suitor, not a secret lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the great sea and its birds fix the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer

103.reading: The friend tells the mother that the lord of the cool ford, where punnai and njaazhal flower together, has become fit for this girl, and her dark beauty has become fit for him alone.
103.nuance: The two trees flowering together look like a hidden image of the matched pair, but it is one correspondence (the pair matched), not two, so it fails condition 3 and is left as scene: a near-miss ullurai. The claim of mutual fitness (அமைந்தனன், அமைந்தன்று) is the friend's argument for marriage put to the mother.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai and njaazhal of the ford mark the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer

104.reading: The friend tells the mother that in their town, at the hour when everyone sleeps, when the girl's beauty had wasted, the rich shore lord came in the dead of night in his well-made chariot, and that town of his is a rich one.
104.nuance: The midnight hour of the kurinji poems is here told to the mother: the secret night visits are themselves part of the disclosure, offered as proof of the lord's devotion and wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: only the shore lord names the land; the poem has no native thing

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; line 1 has வழி for the refrain's வாழி

105.reading: The friend tells the mother that since the lord of the cool ford came, where the waves of the roaring sea bring pearls that glint on the white sand, the girl's brow, look, has turned more golden than gold.
105.nuance: சிவந்தன்று can be read as the glow of joy at his coming or as the gold of pallor (பசலை is gold-coloured in the Akananuru and Kural); read as pallor, the friend names the man as the cause of the change the mother has seen, which is the point of a disclosure.

thinai_evidence.note: the roaring sea, its pearls and the white sand fix the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer

106.reading: The friend tells the mother to look at the girl's lovely chest as she thinks of him: it gleams brighter than the conch of the cool sea in his land, which the swan with its trunk-like legs treads on, taking it for its mate.
106.nuance: The swan that mistakes a white conch for its mate is a near-miss iraicchi: it acts as a lover would, but no single sense for the girl follows from it, so it stays scene. Whether the brightness of her chest is beauty or the whiteness of pallor is not fixed; நினைந்தே ties it to her thoughts of him either way.

thinai_evidence.note: the swan and the sea conch fix the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer

107.reading: The friend tells the mother that her own friend's bright brow has paled, she has wasted and thinned with longing, and whenever she hears the waves breaking on the cool sea she does not sleep, and the friend grieves for it.
107.nuance: The sea's waves, which in other neythal poems carry the lover's chariot, here only keep her awake; the friend reports the symptoms to the mother as her own pain (நோகோ யானே), so the disclosure is also an appeal.

thinai_evidence.note: the breaking waves of the cool sea fix the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; என் தோழி names the girl as the speaker's friend

108.reading: The friend tells the mother that if the lord of the cool sea shore, where the mundakam blooms in the backwater, has abandoned our shoulders, then what are they worth, the shoulders he once desired?
108.nuance: The same shoulders are counted twice, as the ones he has left and the ones he desired: the friend makes the mother see that what he wanted is now thrown away, so the family's honour as well as the girl's is at stake.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, the mundakam and the shore lord fix the coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; the friend says எந்தோள், speaking as one with the girl

109.reading: The friend tells the mother that when the lord of the ford, where neythal with hollow stems spreading on the water is full of flowers, has abandoned our shoulders, what then of the many days he came and showed her his grace?
109.nuance: Paired with 108: there the loss is measured against the shoulders he desired, here against the many days of his grace (அளித்த போழ்தே), so the abandonment is made a breach of a history the mother has not known of.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal of the ford fixes the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; எந்தோள் as in 108

110.reading: The friend tells the mother that we always call the lord of the ford, where the punnai opens its gold-coloured flowers, our own, while this town says something else of him; she asks whether fate, long may it live, will make it so there too.
110.nuance: பால் is the apportioning fate that joins lovers; the friend appeals past the town's talk to it, asking whether it will make the bond real there, in his house and before all, as it already is in their own words (என்னை). Line 4 does not say what the town says, only that it is other.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai of the ford fixes the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து and the address அன்னை make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer

links.note: Both make the cause of love-sickness its cure; in Kural 1102 the man says the girl is the medicine for the sickness she gives, in Ainkurunuru 101 the friend tells the mother the lord's chariot is the medicine for the sickness the girl's eyes caught.
links.teaches: Valluvar states the paradox as the lover's private wonder, while the Sangam friend uses the same paradox as evidence before the mother, so the idea that only the beloved can cure love began as an argument for marriage before it was a maxim of delight.

links.note: In Akananuru 22 the girl laughs inwardly that the velan's rite was wasted when her lover, the true cure, came by night; in Ainkurunuru 101 the friend tells the mother outright that the coming chariot is the cure.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show the same diagnosis moving from the girl's secret mockery of the mother's remedy to the friend's open correction of it, which is the step the disclosure to the mother exists to take.

links.note: In Natrinai 145 the friend tells the girl that the unjust mother suspects them and still the chariot bell comes softly down their street at midnight; in Ainkurunuru 102 the friend tells the mother herself that the chariot bell rings sweetly to end the girl's grief.
links.teaches: The chariot bell is the sound of stealth to be hidden from a suspicious mother in one poem and the sound announced to that mother as relief in the other, so the pair shows the disclosure changing the meaning of the lover's signal from danger to remedy.

links.note: In Akananuru 156 the mother, not knowing the cause, weeps and offers toddy and a goat to the god of the ford while the girl's gem-dark skin turns gold; in Ainkurunuru 105 the friend tells the mother that the girl's brow has gone more golden than gold since the lord came.
links.teaches: The golden pallor that sends the mother to the god in the Akananuru is given its human cause in the Ainkurunuru, so reading them together shows that the friend's disclosure is the answer to the mother's misdirected rite.

links.note: In Natrinai 61 the mother asks the sleepless girl 'don't you sleep, my little one?' and the girl keeps the reason in her heart; in Ainkurunuru 107 the friend tells the mother that the girl does not sleep whenever she hears the waves.
links.teaches: The question the girl will not answer in the Natrinai is answered for her by the friend in the Ainkurunuru, so the pair shows the friend speaking the very secret the girl's modesty withholds from the mother.

links.note: Both open on எந்தோள் துறந்த and ask எவன்கொல்: 108 sets the abandoned shoulders against the shoulders he desired, 109 against the many days of his grace.
links.teaches: Read as a pair, the near-identical poems move the friend's charge from the body he wanted to the time he spent, so the decade builds the case against the lord in two steps, desire then history, before the mother.

links.note: In Kural 1130 the woman says he lives in her heart while this town (இவ் வூர்) says he is loveless and far; in Ainkurunuru 110 the friend says we call him ours while this town (இவ்வூர்) says otherwise, and asks fate to make it so.
links.teaches: Both set the lovers' word against the town's, but Valluvar's woman rests in her inner certainty while the Sangam friend turns to fate to make the bond public, so the couplet's private comfort appears in the older poem as a demand for marriage.

links.note: In Kural 1209 the woman's life fails as she dwells on the lack of grace of one who said they were not apart; in Ainkurunuru 109 the friend asks what the many days of his grace were worth now that he has left.
links.teaches: Valluvar turns the memory of past grace into a slow inward death, while the Sangam friend turns it into a reproach spoken to the mother, so the same memory serves as private lament in the couplet and as public evidence in the decade.

source_issues: 101-110: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the refrain and the decade title.
104: line 1 reads அன்னை வழிவேண் டன்னை where the other nine poems have வாழிவேண்; a dropped vowel sign, likely an e-text slip (not confirmed against another edition).
104: line 4 செல்வனஃ தூரே (செல்வன் அஃது ஊரே) is obscure; whether செல்வன் is 'the rich one' or 'he will go' decides the closing sense.
105, 106: the shown text carries repaired lines (flags in show); the readings follow the repaired text.
